title: Advocate says banning character evidence 'critical' after Western Power rape case

Topic:Sexual Offences

There are moves to abolish character references during sex crime sentencing in WA.  (ABC News: Jack Stevenson)

Advocates and politicians are calling for positive character evidence to be abolished from WA courts for those accused of sexual crimes.

Earlier this year New South Wales abolished good character references in sentencing for sexual offences.

The WA government has committed to outlawing positive character evidence for child sexual assault cases, but is yet to decide whether to do the same for those involving adults.

There are growing calls for the WA government to ban positive character evidence after three Western Power staff were stood down for offering references for a former colleague convicted of rape.

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

As the law stands, judges sentencing offenders can consider references provided to the court which illustrate parts of a person's character.

In the case of former Western Power employee Jeffrey David Spinner, the judge determining the 59-year-old's sentence received eight positive character references which he said illustrated the four counts of rape a jury had found him guilty of was "out of character".

Western Australia's energy minister lashes out at Western Power employees who provided references for a senior manager who was jailed for raping a female colleague.

Judge Massey summarised one Western Power operations manager's statement as saying Spinner had a "strong moral compass", while another colleague described him as always acting "respectfully and appropriately" towards her and others.

A third described him as a "supportive mentor" and a "loyal and dependable friend".

"There's a fairly consistent theme running through those references of you being a very good employee, a dedicated family person and dedicated to your friends as well," Judge Massey summarised.

"So I do give you the benefit of being a person of prior good character."

It contributed to Spinner receiving a five-year jail term.

Those statements stood in stark contrast to the judge's assessment of Spinner's offending against his subordinate — a woman he was mentoring — which was described as "disturbing".

"You essentially did what you wanted with her at a time when you must have thought she was either passed out or asleep," the judge said.

Judge Massey had found the offending happened after the victim felt pressured into going out to dinner with Spinner, which ended with him bringing her to his hotel room, showering her in her clothes and helping her into bed before assaulting her.

Jeffrey David Spinner (right) was sentenced to five years in jail for the rape of a colleague.


  (Facebook: Jeff Spinner)

In her victim impact statement, which also factored into Spinner's sentence, the woman said she "no longer feels safe in the way she once did and consequently assesses whether she can trust the people round her".

"She speaks of feeling scared, vulnerable and uncertain about her future. She no longer sleeps well and is in a near constant state of hyper-vigilance."

The three current Western Power staff who gave Spinner positive character references were all stood down on Tuesday, after the case was brought to the agency's attention by a journalist the afternoon before.

Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the aim was: "To send a message to the organisation and to the community that this behaviour is unacceptable, that this has been a terrible lapse in judgement of those individuals."

Amber-Jade Sanderson at a press conference with Western Power chief Gair Landsborough. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Recently appointed CEO, Gair Landsborough, said he had been unaware of the character references because an oversight meant Western Power staff were not in court when the sentence was handed down and the character references referred to.

"For over two years, we've been supporting our employee," he said.

"She remains part of Western Power's workforce, a real valued contributor, and we want to make sure we continue to support her."

The organisation's handling of the case, communications with the minister and broader culture and safety programs are now all under review.

A survivor advocate behind the campaign calling for good character references to be abolished in sentencing perpetrators of sexual offences has described the NSW reform as "an absolute victory".

And while the state government has committed to outlawing positive character evidence for child sexual assault cases, it is yet to decide whether to do the same for those involving adults.

"Removing these references protects [child] victims from further trauma, ensuring fairness and focusing sentencing on the gravity of the offence rather than the offender's reputation," Attorney General Tony Buti told the ABC in a statement.

"We are currently considering extending this ban to other types of offending."

Earlier this year New South Wales abolished good character references in sentencing for sexual offences.

However, legal figures had raised concerns it could limit the ability of courts to understand "the offender as a whole person".

Alison Evans, from the Centre for Women's Safety and Wellbeing, said it was critical the government banned the practice for adult offenders as well.

"As a state, we are letting victim survivors of sexual violence down if we continue to permit the use of good character references in the courtroom to … influence sexual violence sentencing," she said.

Alison Evans says character references are not reliable evidence.  (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The family and sexual violence advocate said the practice caused a "great deal of harm" to victim-survivors and risked "making them feel that somehow they are to blame".

"Good character references by family, friends, co-workers aren't reliable evidence," she said.

"People who are committing these offences are living, working, socialising amongst us and how we might be perceiving that person can't determine, and we know from the evidence, doesn't determine whether or not they're capable of committing sexual violence."

Greens women and children's safety spokesperson Jess Beckerling agreed.

"Far too many victims of gendered violence are facing the courts and hearing their perpetrator being described as being of good character," she said.

"That's re-traumatising for those victim-survivors, it's outrageous, and it's time that the Cook Labor government just get on and change it."

Ms Beckerling said with parliament scheduled to sit for just nine more weeks before the end of the year, it should be a priority for the government.

Jess Beckerling criticised the government's legislative agenda.  (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"We have a very poor legislative agenda at the moment here in Western Australia," she said.

She said that instead of dealing with "unnecessary administrative bills, we should be dealing with the important things".

"We need to be dealing with this," she said.
